records.source: Καὶ παράγων εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον τυφλὸν ἐκ γενετῆς.
records.gloss: And passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.

L.1: And as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} passed by, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saw a man blind from birth.

R.1: As Jesus was walking along, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saw a man who had been blind since the day he was born.

decisions.choice: passing by: the story moves on from chapter 8 without saying when or where
alternatives: as Jesus left the temple on the same day (8:59)
decisions.reason: John joins the scene to what goes before with a plain "and". Jesus has just left the temple (8:59), but John does not say whether this happened as he left or on another day. The last festival named is Tabernacles (7:2); the next is Dedication (10:22). The man was probably sitting where people passed, since he was a beggar (verse 8).

decisions.choice: blind from birth: he had never seen at all
decisions.reason: The phrase means he was born blind, as the disciples' question (verse 2) and his parents' words (verse 20) confirm. This is the one detail the whole chapter turns on: no one had ever heard of the eyes of a man born blind being opened (verse 32).

decisions.choice: Jesus sees the man first; the man asks for nothing
decisions.reason: As with the man at the pool (5:6), Jesus takes notice of someone who has not called to him. The man cannot see Jesus, and nothing shows he knows who is passing.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: The Greek has no named subject; the last person named is Jesus (8:59). Balanced and Readable name him because a new chapter begins here.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and the man's "he" for Jesus. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

records.heading: Jesus heals a man born blind

records.source: καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ λέγοντες· Ῥαββί, τίς ἥμαρτεν, οὗτος ἢ οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ, ἵνα τυφλὸς γεννηθῇ;
records.gloss: And asked him the disciples of him saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this [one] or the parents of him, that blind he should be born?"

L.2: And {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this [man] or his parents, so that he should be born blind?"

R.2: His disciples asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi, why was this man born blind? Was it because of his own sin, or because his parents sinned?"

decisions.choice: the disciples assume that the blindness must be the result of someone's sin
decisions.reason: Many in Israel held that suffering was punishment for sin. Scripture speaks of God visiting the iniquity of parents on their children (Exodus 20:5; 34:7), and the friends of Job argue that trouble proves guilt (Job 4:7-8). Other passages say that each person bears the guilt of their own sin, not a parent's (Ezekiel 18:20; Jeremiah 31:29-30). Jesus rejects the simple link between disaster and guilt elsewhere too (Luke 13:1-5), though he can warn a man that sin has consequences (5:14).

decisions.choice: this man: the question does not explain how he could have sinned before he was born
alternatives: the disciples hold a worked-out belief that a child can sin in the womb
they assume he lived before his birth
decisions.reason: The disciples offer two possibilities and do not say how the first could be. Some later Jewish writings speak of an unborn child's sin, and others of souls existing before birth, but the text gives no sign that the disciples had any such belief in mind. They may simply be naming every possibility they can think of.

decisions.choice: so that he should be born blind: the result the disciples assume followed from the sin
decisions.reason: The clause has the same form as a purpose clause, but here it states the outcome: whose sin led to his being born blind. Jesus answers with a clause of the same form (verse 3), turning from the cause of the blindness to what God will do.

decisions.choice: Rabbi: a respectful address to a teacher
decisions.reason: The disciples use the Jewish title for a teacher, which John has explained at 1:38. They ask a teacher's ruling on a question of sin and suffering.

decisions.choice: who sinned, so that this man was born blind? (B); why was this man born blind? (R)
alternatives: who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind? (Literal order)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the question first and then the two possibilities, which is easier to follow when read aloud. Readable asks "why", since the disciples want to know the cause (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Οὔτε οὗτος ἥμαρτεν οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἵνα φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus, "Neither this [one] sinned nor the parents of him, but that might be revealed the works of the God in him."

L.3: Jesus answered, "Neither this [man] sinned nor his parents, but [it was] so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

R.3: Jesus answered, "He was not born blind because he sinned or because his parents sinned. It was so that the works of God could be seen in him.

decisions.choice: but so that: a purpose clause whose main verb is left unsaid, looking back to the disciples' question
alternatives: a command: "but let the works of God be revealed in him"
decisions.reason: Jesus answers in few words. The clause beginning "so that" needs something before it, and the nearest thing is the question just asked: he was born blind so that the works of God might be revealed. The same short form, "but so that", stands alone after a denial in 1:8 and 13:18.

decisions.choice: the sentence ends at "in him" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the clause "but so that the works of God might be revealed in him" begins the next sentence: "... so that the works of God may be revealed in him, we must work the works of the one who sent me"
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts have little or no punctuation, so where the sentence ends is a reading of the text. The SBLGNT ends it after "in him", and the next verse begins afresh with "we". Another reading joins the clause to verse 4. John has clauses that open with "but so that" and are completed by what follows (1:31; 14:31), so this is possible. On that reading Jesus says nothing about the purpose of the blindness; he denies that sin caused it and then speaks of the work he and his disciples must do. A footnote gives the other punctuation.

decisions.choice: Jesus rejects sin as the cause in this man's case and points to what God will do in him
alternatives: a general teaching on why people suffer
a statement that God caused the blindness so that he could heal it
decisions.reason: Jesus answers the question asked about "this man" and his parents; he does not lay down a rule for all suffering, and he does not say who or what made the man blind. He turns the question from "why" to "for what": this man's life will show God at work. Readers have long asked how far the purpose clause reaches; the punctuation discussed in m2 is one reason the question remains open.

decisions.choice: the works of God: what God does, seen here in the healing
decisions.reason: In John the "works" are the deeds the Father gives Jesus to do, which show who sent him (5:17, 20, 36; 10:25, 37-38). Verse 4 takes up the same word. To be "revealed" is to be brought into the open, as Jesus's glory was revealed in his first sign (2:11).

decisions.choice: [it was] so that (L); It was so that (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the main verb unsaid (meaning decision m1). Every level supplies the shortest words that make a sentence, and Literal marks them. "It was" keeps as close as possible to the Greek and does not add a statement that God made it happen.

decisions.choice: made visible (B); seen (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something visible that was hidden. Balanced says that in plain words; Readable says what follows from it: people will see God's works in the man.

records.source: ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με ἕως ἡμέρα ἐστίν· ἔρχεται νὺξ ὅτε οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐργάζεσθαι.
records.gloss: Us it is necessary to work the works of the [one] having sent me while day it is; is coming night when no one is able to work.

L.4: It is necessary for us to work the works of the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} while it is day; night is coming, when no one is able to work.

R.4: While it is still day, we must do the works of God, who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Night is coming, and then no one can work.

decisions.choice: we must work ... the one who sent me (SBLGNT)
alternatives: I must work ... the one who sent me (many later manuscripts)
we must work ... the one who sent us (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ on both pronouns. The SBLGNT reads "we" with "me", which is found in early witnesses such as Codex Vaticanus. Many later manuscripts read "I must work", which makes the two pronouns agree; some early ones, among them two early papyri and Codex Sinaiticus as first written, read "sent us", which makes them agree the other way. The uneven "we ... me" is the harder reading, and it is easy to see why copyists would smooth it in either direction. A footnote gives the other readings. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: we: Jesus includes his disciples in the work; the one who sent me is the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus draws the disciples into the work he was sent to do, as he will send them (17:18; 20:21). "The one who sent me" is how he often speaks of the Father in John (5:23-24, 30, 37; 7:16; 8:16, 18, 26, 29).

decisions.choice: must: a necessity that comes from God's purpose
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for what has to happen because God wills it (3:14, 30; 4:4; 10:16; 20:9).

decisions.choice: day and night: the time Jesus is in the world, and the time when it ends
alternatives: an ordinary saying about working hours only
decisions.reason: In a land without artificial light, work stopped at dark. Jesus uses this ordinary fact as a picture: the day is the time while he is present (verse 5; 11:9-10; 12:35-36), and the night is coming, the darkness of his death and of the world without him. When Judas goes out to betray him, John notes "it was night" (13:30).

decisions.choice: While it is still day (first)
alternatives: ... while it is day (at the end, Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the time first, which makes plain that the work must be done now, before night. "Still" brings out the sense that the time is limited (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: God, who sent Me
alternatives: the one who sent Me (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable names the sender, whom Jesus means (meaning decision m2), and ties the works back to "the works of God" in verse 3.

records.source: ὅταν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ὦ, φῶς εἰμι τοῦ κόσμου.
records.gloss: When in the world I am, light I am of the world.

L.5: When I am in the world, I am [the] light of the world."

R.5: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."

decisions.choice: when I am in the world: as long as I am in the world
alternatives: whenever I am in the world
decisions.reason: The word often means "whenever", but with a state that lasts it means "while" or "as long as". It matches the "day" of verse 4: the time Jesus is present in the world is limited.

decisions.choice: light, without the article and placed first: the same claim as in 8:12, with the stress on what he is
decisions.reason: In 8:12 Jesus said "I am the light of the world" with the article and a written-out "I". Here the word "light" stands first, without the article, as a noun often does when it comes before the verb; it still means the one light of the world, not one light among many. The stress falls on "light": what he is about to do for a man in darkness.

decisions.choice: the world: the world of people where Jesus lives and works
decisions.reason: "In the world" is the human world in which Jesus lives for a time (17:11-13). "The light of the world" is light for all people, as in 8:12 and 1:9.

decisions.choice: the saying is about to be acted out in a sign
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats his claim of 8:12 just before he gives sight to a man who has never seen. The healing shows what the saying means, and the chapter ends with Jesus speaking of sight and blindness (9:39-41).

decisions.choice: [the] light (L); the light (B, R)
decisions.reason: Every level says "the light of the world" (meaning decision m2), keeping the same words as 8:12; Literal marks the article as supplied.

records.source: ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἔπτυσεν χαμαὶ καὶ ἐποίησεν πηλὸν ἐκ τοῦ πτύσματος, καὶ ἐπέχρισεν αὐτοῦ τὸν πηλὸν ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ὕπαγε νίψαι εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν τοῦ Σιλωάμ ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Ἀπεσταλμένος.
records.gloss: These things having said, he spat on [the] ground and made mud from the spittle, and smeared of him the mud on the eyes, \v 7 and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of the Siloam" (which is translated Sent).

L.6: Having said these things, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spat on the ground and made mud from the saliva, and smeared the mud on his eyes,
L.7: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which is translated Sent).

R.6: After saying this, Jesus spat on the ground. He mixed the spit with the dirt to make mud, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} put the mud on the man's eyes.
R.7: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him, "Go and wash your face in the pool of Siloam." (Siloam means Sent.)

decisions.choice: smeared (SBLGNT)
alternatives: put (Codex Vaticanus and a few others)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts have a verb meaning to smear or rub on, which is related to the verb for anointing; the man uses it again in verse 11. A few, among them Codex Vaticanus, have the ordinary verb "put on", which the man uses when he tells the story again in verse 15. The meaning is much the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: saliva and mud: means of healing that people of the time recognized
decisions.reason: Jesus uses saliva in two healings in Mark (7:33; 8:23, the second for a blind man). Ancient writers also report saliva used against eye disease; Tacitus tells of a blind man in Alexandria who asked the emperor Vespasian to touch his eyes with spittle (Histories 4.81). Jesus does not heal by the mud, though: he sends the man to wash it off. Kneading was among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2), and making the mud becomes the charge in verse 14.

decisions.choice: possibly an echo of God forming the first man from the ground (Genesis 2:7)
alternatives: no allusion; the mud is simply the means used
decisions.reason: Jesus makes mud from the ground and puts it where the man's eyes had never worked, which some readers take as a picture of the Creator finishing what was lacking from birth (compare Job 10:9; Isaiah 64:8, where God shapes people as from clay). John does not point to Genesis, and the Greek Old Testament uses a different word there (dust), so the link is possible but not certain.

decisions.choice: the pool of Siloam: a pool at the south end of Jerusalem, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel
decisions.reason: King Hezekiah cut a tunnel through the rock to bring the water of the Gihon spring inside the city wall (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30); Isaiah speaks of the gently flowing waters of Shiloah (Isaiah 8:6). A large pool with steps from the time of Jesus has been uncovered at the south end of the old city of David. Later Jewish tradition (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9) says that during the Festival of Tabernacles water was drawn from Siloam and poured out at the altar, which may lie behind Jesus's words about living water at that feast (7:37-38).

decisions.choice: which is translated Sent: John explains the meaning of the Hebrew name
alternatives: the words are part of what Jesus said
decisions.reason: As at 1:38, 1:41 and 1:42, John translates a Hebrew word for his readers; the explanation is the narrator's, not part of Jesus's command. The name comes from a verb meaning "send", probably because the water was sent into the pool through the channel.

decisions.choice: Sent: the man washes in the pool named for the one God sent
decisions.reason: John gives the meaning of the name because it matters: Jesus calls God "the one who sent me" (verse 4) and is himself the one sent by the Father (3:17, 34; 5:36-38; 10:36). The man is sent to the "Sent" pool by the Sent One, and he sees.

decisions.choice: mud
decisions.reason: The word means wet earth, mud or clay. "Mud" is what spittle and dust make; "clay" suggests a potter's material and leans toward the creation reading, which is uncertain (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: smeared (L); spread (B); put (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is related to the one for anointing, but here it describes rubbing mud on, with nothing ceremonial about it. "Anointed" would suggest oil and ritual.

decisions.choice: the explanation stands outside the quotation marks
decisions.reason: The explanation of the name is John's own (meaning decision m5), so every level places it after Jesus's words, as 1:42 does. Balanced and Readable say "means" rather than "is translated".

decisions.choice: Jesus; mixed the spit with the dirt; wash your face
alternatives: he; made mud from the saliva; wash
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, says how the mud was made from the saliva and the ground, and says what the man was to wash: the mud off his eyes, which the story implies.

records.source: ἀπῆλθεν οὖν καὶ ἐνίψατο, καὶ ἦλθεν βλέπων.
records.gloss: He went away therefore and washed, and came seeing.

L.7: So he went away and washed, and came [back] seeing.

R.7: So the man went and washed his face. When he came back, he could see!

decisions.choice: he went, washed and came back seeing: he did exactly what he was told
decisions.reason: The three verbs follow Jesus's command step by step: go, wash, and then the result. "Came seeing" means he returned able to see. John does not say where he came back to; Jesus is not there when he returns (verse 12), and it is his neighbors who meet him (verse 8).

decisions.choice: a man sent to wash and healed when he obeys, as Naaman was (2 Kings 5:10-14)
decisions.reason: Elisha sent Naaman to wash in the Jordan, and he was healed when he did so. The pattern is similar: the healer is not present, and the healing comes with the washing done in obedience. John does not mention Naaman, so the link is a likely echo, not a certain one.

decisions.choice: seeing: for the first time in his life
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for seeing, but for a man blind from birth (verse 1) it means sight he never had. The healing comes away from Jesus, as with the official's son (4:50-53).

decisions.choice: [back] (L); the man ... back (B); the man ... his face ... When he came back (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means "came"; in context it means he came back, and Literal marks the word. Balanced and Readable name the man so that he is not confused with Jesus, and Readable repeats "his face" from verse 7a.

records.source: οἱ οὖν γείτονες καὶ οἱ θεωροῦντες αὐτὸν τὸ πρότερον ὅτι προσαίτης ἦν ἔλεγον· Οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ καθήμενος καὶ προσαιτῶν;
records.gloss: The therefore neighbors and those seeing him the formerly that a beggar he was were saying, "Not this is the [one] sitting and begging?"

L.8: So the neighbors and those who had seen him before, that he was a beggar, were saying, "Is this not the one who sat and begged?"

R.8: His neighbors and other people who had seen him begging before kept asking, "Is this not the beggar who used to sit there?"

decisions.choice: a beggar (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The early manuscripts say people had seen him as a beggar; many later ones say they had seen that he was blind. Both are true of the man; the SBLGNT reading fits the question that follows, "the one who sat and begged". A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a blind man had little way to live except by begging
decisions.reason: With no means of earning a living, the blind and the lame often sat by roads, city gates or the temple entrance asking for alms (Mark 10:46; Acts 3:2). Everyone in the area would know this man by sight.

decisions.choice: were saying: they began to say, and the talk went round
decisions.reason: The imperfect pictures people talking it over among themselves, one after another, as the next verse shows.

decisions.choice: Is this not ...?: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: The form of the question shows that those asking think it is the same man but can hardly believe it.

decisions.choice: began asking (B); kept asking (R); the beggar who used to sit there (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the ongoing talk (meaning decision m3). Readable puts the man's place in one plain phrase.

records.source: ἄλλοι ἔλεγον ὅτι Οὗτός ἐστιν· ἄλλοι ἔλεγον· Οὐχί, ἀλλὰ ὅμοιος αὐτῷ ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Others were saying, "This [one] is"; others were saying, "No, but like him he is."

L.9: Others were saying, "This is [he]"; others were saying, "No, but he is like him."

R.9: Some said, "Yes, it is the same man." Others said, "No, it is just someone who looks like him."

decisions.choice: others ... others: the people divide into two groups
decisions.reason: The repeated word sets one group against the other. Some of those in verse 8 say it is the man; some say it only looks like him.

decisions.choice: like him: someone who looks like the beggar
decisions.reason: A man who now looks about him and walks freely may look different from the beggar who sat with closed or clouded eyes, so some cannot believe it is he.

decisions.choice: the first of several divisions over the sign
decisions.reason: The people are divided, as crowds were over Jesus before (7:12, 43). The division grows sharper among the Pharisees (9:16) and among the crowd once more (10:19-21).

decisions.choice: Some ... Others (B, R); That is the man (B); Yes, it is the same man (R)
decisions.reason: "Some ... others" is the natural way to set two groups side by side. Balanced and Readable say plainly what "this is" means here.

records.source: ἐκεῖνος ἔλεγεν ὅτι Ἐγώ εἰμι.
records.gloss: That [one] was saying, "I am [he]."

R.9: But the man kept telling them, "Yes, it is me!"

decisions.choice: I am: "I am the man", a plain answer about who he is
alternatives: an echo of the divine name
decisions.reason: The words are the ones Jesus uses of himself (6:20; 8:24, 28, 58), but here they are spoken by the healed man and mean simply "I am the one you are talking about". The words to be supplied come from the question of verse 8. John may let a reader hear the same words in the man's mouth, but nothing in the text makes them more than an answer to his neighbors.

decisions.choice: that one kept saying: the man himself, against the doubters
decisions.reason: The pronoun singles him out from the people talking about him, and the imperfect shows that he had to say it again and again.

decisions.choice: That [man] ... [he] (L); The man himself ... the one (B); the man ... it is me (R)
decisions.reason: "I am" alone would sound like an unfinished sentence or suggest more than the man means (meaning decision m1). Every level completes it, and Literal marks the words. Readable uses the everyday "it is me" rather than the formal "it is I".

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν αὐτῷ· Πῶς ἠνεῴχθησάν σου οἱ ὀφθαλμοί;
records.gloss: They were saying therefore to him, "How were opened of you the eyes?"

L.10: So they were saying to him, "How were your eyes opened?"

R.10: So they asked him, "How did your eyes get opened? How can you see now?"

decisions.choice: your eyes were opened: you were given sight
decisions.reason: To open the eyes of the blind is to give them sight. The phrase runs through the chapter (verses 14, 17, 21, 26, 30, 32) and into 10:21.

decisions.choice: opening the eyes of the blind: a work Scripture gives to God
decisions.reason: The prophets name the opening of blind eyes among the things God will do when he comes to save his people (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7), and a psalm says that the LORD opens the eyes of the blind (Psalm 146:8). The neighbors do not draw this out, but the man will later reason that only one from God could do it (verses 32-33).

decisions.choice: how: they ask about the means, and the passive leaves the doer unnamed
decisions.reason: The question is how it happened, and by implication who did it. The imperfect "were saying" again shows several people pressing the question.

decisions.choice: How can you see now?
decisions.reason: Readable adds a plain question that says what "your eyes were opened" means (meaning decision m1), keeping the phrase itself because it recurs through the chapter.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη ἐκεῖνος· Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ λεγόμενος Ἰησοῦς πηλὸν ἐποίησεν καὶ ἐπέχρισέν μου τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἶπέν μοι ὅτι Ὕπαγε εἰς τὸν Σιλωὰμ καὶ νίψαι· ἀπελθὼν οὖν καὶ νιψάμενος ἀνέβλεψα.
records.gloss: Answered that [one], "The man the [one] being called Jesus mud made and smeared of me the eyes and said to me that, 'Go to the Siloam and wash'; having gone therefore and having washed, I received sight."

L.11: He answered, "The man who is called Jesus made mud and smeared my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So having gone and having washed, I received sight."

R.11: He answered, "The man named Jesus made some mud and put it on my eyes. He told me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went there and washed, and now I can see!"

decisions.choice: the man called Jesus: he knows nothing about Jesus but his name
alternatives: a title showing that he already believes in Jesus
decisions.reason: The man never saw Jesus, and Jesus was gone when he came back (verse 12). He speaks of "the man" and gives the name he heard. His understanding grows through the chapter: a prophet (verse 17), a man from God (verse 33), and at last the Son of Man, whom he calls Lord and worships (verses 35-38).

decisions.choice: I received sight: he gained sight he never had
decisions.reason: The verb can mean "look up" or "see again", but it is the usual word for the blind receiving sight (Matthew 11:5), whether or not they had seen before. This man was born blind (verse 1), so it means he could see for the first time.

decisions.choice: to Siloam (SBLGNT)
alternatives: to the pool of Siloam (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts make the man's words match verse 7 by adding "the pool of". The early manuscripts have the shorter wording. The meaning is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a short report in the order things happened
decisions.reason: The man tells only what he felt and heard: the mud, the command, the washing, the sight. He leaves out the spitting, which he could not see, and the meaning of the name Siloam, which is John's comment (verse 7).

decisions.choice: The man named Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the man's own way of speaking (meaning decision m1) and give him no more knowledge of Jesus than the story allows.

decisions.choice: I received sight (L); I began to see (B); now I can see (R)
decisions.reason: Every level avoids "again" and "regained", since he had never seen (meaning decision m2).

records.source: καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Ποῦ ἐστιν ἐκεῖνος;
records.gloss: And they said to him, "Where is that [one]?"

L.12: And they said to him, "Where is that [one]?"

decisions.choice: that one: the man he has just named, who is not there
decisions.reason: The pronoun points to someone at a distance, here the Jesus of whom the healed man has spoken. It is not hostile in itself; later the Pharisees use the same word with scorn (verse 28).

decisions.choice: Jesus is absent from the scene
decisions.reason: From verse 8 to verse 34 Jesus does not appear. The man has to answer for him without him, and Jesus finds him again only after he has been thrown out (verse 35), as he found the healed man in 5:14.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the ordinary pronoun, which in natural speech carries the same sense of someone absent; Readable adds "now".

records.source: λέγει· Οὐκ οἶδα.
records.gloss: He says, "Not I know."

decisions.choice: I do not know: he has never seen Jesus and does not know where he went
decisions.reason: He was blind when Jesus spoke to him and Jesus was gone when he came back, so he could not even recognize him. He says no more than he knows, as he will again in verse 25.

decisions.choice: he says: a present tense in a story told in the past
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present ("he says") to make a scene vivid. It brings the short exchange to a close; it does not change the time.

decisions.choice: he said (B); he answered (R)
decisions.reason: John's present tense (meaning decision m2) is kept in Literal; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This is the only such verb in the passage.

records.source: Ἄγουσιν αὐτὸν πρὸς τοὺς Φαρισαίους τόν ποτε τυφλόν.
records.gloss: They bring him to the Pharisees, the once blind [one].

L.13: They bring him to the Pharisees, the [man who was] once blind.

R.13: Some people took the man who used to be blind to the Pharisees.

decisions.choice: they: the people who had questioned the man, left unnamed
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. The nearest people in the story are the neighbors and those who had seen him begging, who asked how his eyes were opened and where Jesus was (9:8-12). John does not say who brought him or why.

decisions.choice: the Pharisees: here acting as the men with authority to judge the matter
alternatives: a formal session of the council
decisions.reason: The Pharisees were a movement devoted to studying the law of Moses and keeping it in detail, the Sabbath included. In John they act with the chief priests against Jesus (7:32, 45-48). Here they question the man and his parents and decide what to do about those who confess Jesus (9:22, 34). John does not say whether this was a formal court.

decisions.choice: the once blind: named by what he had been
decisions.reason: John identifies the man by his past: the one who was blind before. The phrase keeps the wonder of what has happened in view as the questioning begins.

decisions.choice: They bring (L); took (B, R)
decisions.reason: John tells this in the present tense, the historic present, as he often does; it happens again in 9:17 ("they say"). Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English tells a story. This decision covers both verbs in the passage.

decisions.choice: Some people
decisions.reason: Readable gives the verb a subject, since a plain "they" has nothing to point back to at the start of a new scene. It does not say who they were (meaning decision m1).

records.heading: The Pharisees question the man

records.source: ἦν δὲ σάββατον ἐν ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ τὸν πηλὸν ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ἀνέῳξεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς.
records.gloss: Was now Sabbath on which day the mud made the Jesus and opened of him the eyes.

L.14: Now it was Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.

R.14: Jesus made the mud and opened the man's eyes on a Sabbath, the weekly day of rest.

decisions.choice: a late remark that turns the story
decisions.reason: As in 5:9, John mentions the day only after the healing is told. The remark explains why the Pharisees take up the matter and sets up the dispute of verse 16.

decisions.choice: making mud: work forbidden on the Sabbath, as the Pharisees understood it
decisions.reason: God forbade Israel to do any work on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8-11). Later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah about AD 200, lists kneading among the main kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Shabbat 7:2); mixing earth and saliva into mud could count as kneading. John names the making of the mud, not only the healing, as the thing done on that day.

decisions.choice: opened his eyes: a healing where no life was in danger
decisions.reason: Later Jewish teaching allowed treatment on the Sabbath when a life was in danger (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). A man blind from birth was in no danger, so by that rule the healing could have waited a day. Jesus had already answered such a charge in 7:21-24.

decisions.choice: the mud: the wet earth Jesus made with his saliva
decisions.reason: The article points back to 9:6, where Jesus spat on the ground and made mud. The word means wet earth or clay; here it is a paste put on the man's eyes.

decisions.choice: it was on a Sabbath that (B); ... on a Sabbath (R)
alternatives: Now it was Sabbath on the day when (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the stress on the day with "it was on a Sabbath that"; Readable tells the deed first and ends on the day, which is what matters for the dispute.

decisions.choice: the weekly day of rest; the man's eyes
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word Sabbath, as at 5:9, and says whose eyes, since "his" right after Jesus could be misread.

records.source: πάλιν οὖν ἠρώτων αὐτὸν καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι πῶς ἀνέβλεψεν.
records.gloss: Again therefore were asking him also the Pharisees how he received sight.

L.15: So again the Pharisees also were asking him how he had received sight.

R.15: So now the Pharisees also asked him how he had become able to see.

decisions.choice: again ... also: the Pharisees ask what the neighbors had asked
alternatives: the Pharisees asked him a second time
decisions.reason: The neighbors had already asked how his eyes were opened (9:10). "Again" and "also" mark that the Pharisees now put the same question; they had not asked before in the story.

decisions.choice: received sight: came to see
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to look up or to see again. The man was born blind (9:1), so here it simply means to gain sight, as in 9:11 and 9:18.

decisions.choice: were asking: questioning, perhaps pressing him
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect. It may simply set the scene of an exchange, or picture them pressing him with questions.

decisions.choice: in turn (B); now ... also (R)
decisions.reason: "Again" here means that the question is asked a second time in the story, not that the Pharisees repeat their own question (meaning decision m1); Balanced and Readable avoid a word that would suggest that.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Πηλὸν ἐπέθηκέν μου ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, καὶ ἐνιψάμην, καὶ βλέπω.
records.gloss: He but said to them, "Mud he put of me on the eyes, and I washed, and I see."

L.15: And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."

R.15: He told them, "He put mud on my eyes. Then I washed, and now I can see."

decisions.choice: a shorter account than in 9:11
decisions.reason: To the neighbors the man named "the man called Jesus", told of the mud, the command to go to Siloam, and his washing (9:11). To the Pharisees he says only three things in three short clauses. John gives no reason for the shorter answer.

decisions.choice: he: Jesus, not named
decisions.reason: The man does not name his healer here. The Pharisees know whom he means, and in verse 17 they ask about "him".

decisions.choice: I see: a present that lasts
decisions.reason: After two past actions the last verb is present: he sees now, and goes on seeing. The healing is not a passing moment.

decisions.choice: I can see now (B); now I can see (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "now" and "can" to bring out the present state after the past actions (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: He (plain, at the start of the quotation)
decisions.reason: The pronoun for Jesus starts the man's words, so it is capitalized either way and written plain.

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων τινές· Οὐκ ἔστιν οὗτος παρὰ θεοῦ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὅτι τὸ σάββατον οὐ τηρεῖ.
records.gloss: Were saying therefore of the Pharisees some, "Not is this from God the man, because the Sabbath not he keeps."

L.16: So some of the Pharisees were saying, "This man is not from God, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} does not keep the Sabbath."

R.16: Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God. He does not keep the Sabbath."

decisions.choice: from God: sent by God and acting with his authority
decisions.reason: To be "from God" is to come with God's commission. Nicodemus said that no one could do these signs unless God were with him (3:2), and the healed man will argue that if Jesus were not from God he could do nothing (9:33).

decisions.choice: their reasoning: one who breaks the Sabbath cannot be sent by God
decisions.reason: The law warned that a prophet who gave a sign and then led the people away from God's commands was not to be followed (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). These Pharisees start from the Sabbath: if Jesus broke it, whatever he did, he cannot come from God. Jesus had answered that charge before (5:17; 7:22-23).

decisions.choice: keep: observe, obey
decisions.reason: The verb means to keep or observe a command. The Pharisees judge Jesus by their own understanding of what the Sabbath forbids (meaning decision m2 at 9:14).

decisions.choice: this man: a distant, perhaps scornful way to speak of him
decisions.reason: They do not use Jesus's name but "this ... the man", with the words split for emphasis. It may carry a note of disdain, as in 5:12.

decisions.choice: two sentences, without "because"
alternatives: because he does not keep the Sabbath
decisions.reason: Readable gives the charge as its own sentence; the reason is still plain from the order.

records.source: ἄλλοι ἔλεγον· Πῶς δύναται ἄνθρωπος ἁμαρτωλὸς τοιαῦτα σημεῖα ποιεῖν;
records.gloss: Others were saying, "How is able a man sinful such signs to do?"

L.16: Others were saying, "How is a man who is a sinner able to do such signs?"

R.16: But other Pharisees said, "A man who is a sinner could not do signs like these!"

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer: he cannot
decisions.reason: The question is not a request for information. It means that a sinner could not do such things. These Pharisees reason from the signs to the man, where the first group reasoned from the Sabbath to the man.

decisions.choice: a sinner: one who breaks God's law
decisions.reason: The word takes up the first group's charge: by breaking the Sabbath Jesus would be a sinner. The same word comes back in 9:24-25 and 9:31.

decisions.choice: such signs: deeds that point to God at work
decisions.reason: John calls Jesus's deeds signs (2:11; 4:54). A sign shows who the doer is; to these Pharisees the healing of a man born blind shows that God is with Jesus, as Nicodemus said in 3:2.

decisions.choice: others: other Pharisees
decisions.reason: "Others" stands against "some of the Pharisees" just before, and the next sentence says the division was "among them". These are Pharisees too.

decisions.choice: other Pharisees ... could not do signs like these!
alternatives: How is a man who is a sinner able to do such signs? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects as a plain statement (meaning decision m1) and says who "others" were (meaning decision m4). Balanced keeps the question.

records.source: καὶ σχίσμα ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: And a division was among them.

L.16: And there was a division among them.

R.16: So the Pharisees were split into two sides.

decisions.choice: division: a split into opposing sides
decisions.reason: The word (σχίσμα) is used of a tear in cloth; John uses it of people who split into camps over Jesus, as the crowd did in 7:43 and the Jews will in 10:19.

decisions.choice: among them: even the Pharisees are divided by Jesus
decisions.reason: In 7:43 the crowd was split; now the men who judge the matter are split as well. In John people divide over who Jesus is (7:40-43; 9:39).

decisions.choice: they were divided (B); were split into two sides (R)
alternatives: there was a division among them (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the noun into a verb. Readable names the Pharisees and says "two sides", since the verse has just set out two views.

records.source: λέγουσιν οὖν τῷ τυφλῷ πάλιν· Τί σὺ λέγεις περὶ αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἠνέῳξέν σου τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς;
records.gloss: They say therefore to the blind [man] again, "What you say about him, because he opened of you the eyes?"
pieces: the man who had been blind

L.17: So they say to the blind [man] again, "What do you say about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, since {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} opened your eyes?"

R.17: So they spoke to the man again. "What do you say about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?" they asked. "After all, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} opened your eyes."

decisions.choice: you: emphatic, you of all people
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out, which in Greek gives it weight. Since the healing was done to him, the Pharisees, divided among themselves, ask for his view.

decisions.choice: since: giving the reason for asking
alternatives: that: "What do you say about him, that he opened your eyes?"
decisions.reason: The small word can give a reason ("since he opened your eyes") or state what they ask about ("what do you say about this, that he opened your eyes?"). The sense is close either way: they ask him to judge Jesus by what happened to him.

decisions.choice: the blind [man]: John still names him by what he had been
decisions.reason: John goes on calling him "the blind man" though he can now see, as in 9:13.

decisions.choice: the man who had been blind; And you (B); After all (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "who had been" so that "blind" is not misread as his present state, and "And you" carries the weight of the written-out pronoun (meaning decision m1). Readable puts the reason in its own sentence with "After all". Literal keeps the present "they say" (see the decision on the historic present at 9:13).

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν ὅτι Προφήτης ἐστίν.
records.gloss: He but said that, "A prophet he is."

L.17: And he said, "He is a prophet."

R.17: The man answered, "He is a prophet."

decisions.choice: a prophet: a man sent by God to speak for him
decisions.reason: The word has no article: he says "a prophet", not "the Prophet" the crowd spoke of in 7:40. Prophets of Israel such as Elijah and Elisha were known for healings done by God's power (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 5:1-14). The Samaritan woman came to the same view (4:19).

decisions.choice: a step in the man's growing understanding
decisions.reason: He first spoke of "the man called Jesus" (9:11); now he calls him a prophet; later he argues that Jesus is from God (9:33), and at last believes in him as the Son of Man and worships him (9:35-38).

decisions.choice: that: introduces his words
decisions.reason: The small word here simply opens a quotation, like quotation marks.

decisions.choice: The man
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker, since the sentence that follows has another "he" for Jesus.

decisions.choice: a prophet, lowercase
decisions.reason: The capital is kept for the expected figure of 1:21 and 7:40; here the man means a prophet like those of old (meaning decision m1). "He" for Jesus starts the quotation, so it is written plain.

records.source: Οὐκ ἐπίστευσαν οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι περὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι ἦν τυφλὸς καὶ ἀνέβλεψεν, ἕως ὅτου ἐφώνησαν τοὺς γονεῖς αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀναβλέψαντος καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτοὺς λέγοντες· Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμῶν, ὃν ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη;
records.gloss: Not believed therefore the Jews about him that he was blind and received sight, until that they called the parents of him, of the [one] having received sight, \v 19 and asked them saying, "This is the son of you, whom you say that blind he was born?

L.18: So the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight, until they called his parents, [the parents] of the one who had received sight,
L.19: and asked them, saying, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind?

R.18: The Jewish leaders would not believe that the man had been blind and could now see until they had called for his parents.
R.19: They asked them, "Is this your son? Are you saying he was born blind?

decisions.choice: the Jews: the same Pharisees and authorities as in verses 13-17
alternatives: a different group from the Pharisees
decisions.reason: John switches from "the Pharisees" to "the Jews" without a break in the story. The people meant are those who have been questioning the man and who will question his parents, in other words the authorities. It is not the people as a whole: the man and his parents are Jews too, and so is Jesus.

decisions.choice: until: their disbelief held until the parents were called
decisions.reason: They refused to accept the healing as fact and looked for witnesses. Parents could say who their son was and whether he had been blind from birth, which no one else could prove.

decisions.choice: you say: emphatic, putting the claim on them
decisions.reason: The "you" is written out: "whom you say". The question treats the blindness from birth as the parents' claim, as if it might be false, and so presses them to answer for it.

decisions.choice: the one who had received sight: John keeps the healing in view
decisions.reason: Even as he tells of their disbelief, John names the man by what has happened to him. The words added after "his parents" stress the point.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: summoned the parents of the man who could now see (B); called for his parents (R)
alternatives: called his parents, [the parents] of the one who had received sight (Literal)
decisions.reason: The Greek names the parents twice over ("his parents, of the one who had received sight"); Balanced folds the two into one phrase, and Readable keeps only "his parents". Readable splits the question in two.

records.source: πῶς οὖν βλέπει ἄρτι;
records.gloss: How therefore does he see now?"

L.19: How then does he see now?"

R.19: Then how can he see now?"

decisions.choice: how then: a second question that follows from the first
decisions.reason: If he is their son and was born blind, then the parents must account for his sight. The question asks the parents to explain what the man has already explained (9:15).

decisions.choice: now: at this moment, in contrast to his birth
decisions.reason: The word stands against "born blind": blind then, seeing now.

decisions.choice: is able to see (B); can see (R)
decisions.reason: The plain present "sees" sounds odd in English here; "can see" says the same thing.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθησαν οὖν οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ εἶπαν· Οἴδαμεν ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη·
records.gloss: Answered therefore the parents of him and said, "We know that this is the son of us and that blind he was born;

L.20: So his parents answered and said, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.

R.20: His parents answered, "We know this is our son. And we know he was born blind.

decisions.choice: they answer only what they can witness to
decisions.reason: They answer the first question and confirm the two facts that only parents could swear to: who he is and that he was born blind. That settles what the authorities doubted (verse 18).

decisions.choice: we know: set against "we do not know" in verse 21
decisions.reason: The parents set out carefully what they know and what they say they do not know. The pairing prepares for John's explanation in verse 22.

decisions.choice: answered and said: one act of speaking
decisions.reason: The pair of verbs is a common biblical way to introduce a reply; it does not mean two separate acts.

decisions.choice: answered
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use one verb (meaning decision m3). Both repeat "we know" before the second fact, and Readable "we know" so that each fact has its own short sentence.

records.source: πῶς δὲ νῦν βλέπει οὐκ οἴδαμεν, ἢ τίς ἤνοιξεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἡμεῖς οὐκ οἴδαμεν· αὐτὸν ἐρωτήσατε, ἡλικίαν ἔχει, αὐτὸς περὶ ἑαυτοῦ λαλήσει.
records.gloss: How but now he sees not we know, or who opened of him the eyes we not know; him ask, age he has, he about himself will speak."

L.21: But how he now sees we do not know, or who opened his eyes we do not know. Ask him; he is of age; he himself will speak about himself."

R.21: But we do not know how he can see now, or who opened his eyes. Ask him. He is a grown man. He can speak for himself."

decisions.choice: he is of age: he is an adult, old enough to answer for himself
decisions.reason: The phrase means to have reached full age. As an adult the man could be questioned in his own right and give his own testimony; his parents need not answer for him. Later Jewish teaching counted a boy responsible for keeping the commandments from age thirteen (Mishnah Avot 5:21); the man here is plainly a grown man.

decisions.choice: we ... him ... he himself: the parents hand the questions back to their son
decisions.reason: "We" is written out in the second "we do not know", "him" comes first in "ask him", and "he" and "himself" are stressed in the last clause. Each word pushes responsibility away from the parents and onto the son.

decisions.choice: who opened his eyes: they say they do not know
decisions.reason: The parents claim not to know who healed him. Verse 22 explains why they speak so carefully; John does not say whether they knew or had heard the name of Jesus.

decisions.choice: of age and can answer for himself (B); He is a grown man. He can speak for himself. (R)
alternatives: He is of age; he will speak for himself (Literal)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "of age" means (meaning decision m1). "Can" at Balanced and Readable brings out that he is able to answer, which is the point of the parents' remark.

records.source: ταῦτα εἶπαν οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ ὅτι ἐφοβοῦντο τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, ἤδη γὰρ συνετέθειντο οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἵνα ἐάν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χριστόν, ἀποσυνάγωγος γένηται.
records.gloss: These things said the parents of him because they were fearing the Jews, already for had agreed the Jews that if anyone him confessed Christ, out-of-the-synagogue he would become.

L.22: His parents said these things because they were afraid of the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [to be the] {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, {{gender:they|he}} would be put out of the synagogue.

R.22: His parents answered like this because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders. The leaders had already agreed together that if anyone openly said Jesus was the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, that person would be thrown out of the synagogue.

decisions.choice: the Jews (twice): the authorities
decisions.reason: Both times the word means the leaders who were questioning the man, the same group called Pharisees in verses 13-16. It cannot mean the people as a whole: the parents who fear them are Jews themselves, and so are the man and Jesus. Those who "agreed" on a penalty are men with power over the synagogue.

decisions.choice: put out of the synagogue: shut out of the community's worship and common life
alternatives: a formal, written ban in force across the land
no more than an informal threat
decisions.reason: The word (ἀποσυνάγωγος) is found in the New Testament only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). The synagogue was where Jews met each Sabbath for prayer and the reading of Scripture, and it was also the center of the town's shared life, so to be put out of it was to be cut off from one's people. Later Jewish sources speak of synagogue discipline that shut a person out for a time. No source outside John records a measure in Jesus's lifetime against those who confessed him; the verse speaks of an agreement among the leaders, and how formal it was and how far it reached is not known.

decisions.choice: confess: say openly, acknowledge in public
decisions.reason: The verb means to declare openly what one holds to be true. John the Baptist "confessed" that he was not the Christ (1:20); in 12:42 some rulers believed in Jesus but would not confess it for fear of being put out of the synagogue.

decisions.choice: had already agreed: a decision taken before this hearing
decisions.reason: The verb is in a past-before-past tense with "already": the leaders had agreed on the penalty before the parents were called. People were afraid to speak openly about Jesus for fear of these authorities as early as 7:13.

decisions.choice: him ... Christ: confessing that he is the Christ
decisions.reason: "Christ" here has no article in Greek; it states what the person would confess Jesus to be. It is the title, the anointed king Israel was waiting for (1:41; 7:41), not a name.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: [to be the] {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); as the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (B); was the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (R); {{gender:they|he}} (L)
decisions.reason: "Christ" is the title (meaning decision m5), so every level writes "the" before the setting, Literal in brackets because the Greek has no article. "Anyone" means a man or a woman, so the pronoun after it in Literal carries the gender setting; Balanced says "anyone who" and Readable "that person", which need none. Balanced joins the two mentions of the leaders with "who".

decisions.choice: openly said Jesus was
decisions.reason: Readable explains "confess" (meaning decision m3) and names Jesus for "him", since the nearest "him" is the parents' son.

records.source: διὰ τοῦτο οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ εἶπαν ὅτι Ἡλικίαν ἔχει, αὐτὸν ἐπερωτήσατε.
records.gloss: Because of this the parents of him said that, "Age he has, him ask."

L.23: Because of this his parents said, "He is of age; ask him."

R.23: That is why his parents said, "He is a grown man. Ask him."

decisions.choice: the parents' words repeated in reverse order
decisions.reason: In verse 21 they said "Ask him; he is of age"; John now quotes the words the other way round. The repetition closes the explanation that began in verse 22 and returns to the story.

decisions.choice: ask: the same request as in verse 21
decisions.reason: The verb here has a prefix the one in verse 21 lacks, but the sense is the same: question him.

decisions.choice: Question him (B); a grown man (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "question" for the longer verb (meaning decision m2). As in verse 21, Readable says plainly what "of age" means.

records.source: Ἐφώνησαν οὖν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐκ δευτέρου ὃς ἦν τυφλὸς καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Δὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ· ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν ὅτι οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἁμαρτωλός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: They called therefore the man out of second [time] who was blind, and said to him, "Give glory to the God; we know that this the man a sinner is."

L.24: So for a second [time] they called the man who had been blind, and said to him, "Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner."

R.24: So the Jewish leaders called back the man who had been blind. They said to him, "Give glory to God by telling the truth! We know that this man is a sinner."

decisions.choice: Give glory to God: a solemn charge to tell the truth in God's presence
alternatives: give God, not Jesus, the praise for the healing
decisions.reason: The words are a set formula for putting someone under oath. Joshua says them to Achan before Achan confesses what he had taken (Joshua 7:19), and the sense there is: own the truth before God, who sees it. The leaders demand that the man stop defending the healer and admit what they think is the truth. Some read the words as "thank God for your sight, not this man", and that thought may be present as well, but the formula and the setting of a hearing point first to the oath. A footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: glory: the honor that belongs to God
decisions.reason: Key term. To give God glory is to honor him as he deserves; here that means honoring him by speaking the truth before him (meaning decision m1). The irony is that the man's honest testimony is exactly what gives God glory (compare 9:3, so that the works of God might be shown in him).

decisions.choice: we know: the pronoun is emphatic; the leaders speak with the authority of teachers of the law
decisions.reason: They set their verdict against the man's story: whatever happened, they know what Jesus is. The phrase "we know" runs through the rest of the passage. The man answers that he does not know this (9:25); they claim to know that God spoke to Moses but not where Jesus comes from (9:29); and the man turns their words back on them (9:31).

decisions.choice: a sinner: one who breaks God's law, here by working on the Sabbath
alternatives: a sinner in the general sense that all people sin
decisions.reason: Some of the Pharisees had already said that Jesus was not from God because he did not keep the Sabbath (9:14-16). He had made mud and healed on that day. For them this settled the matter: a man who breaks the law in this way is a sinner and cannot have been sent by God.

decisions.choice: a second time: the leaders call the man back after questioning his parents
decisions.reason: They had questioned him once (9:15-17), and then his parents (9:18-23). Now they call him in again.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders; by telling the truth
decisions.reason: Readable names the speakers, the authorities who questioned the man and his parents (9:13-23), and says what the formula "give glory to God" asks of him (meaning decision m1). It keeps the word "glory".

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη οὖν ἐκεῖνος· Εἰ ἁμαρτωλός ἐστιν οὐκ οἶδα· ἓν οἶδα ὅτι τυφλὸς ὢν ἄρτι βλέπω.
records.gloss: Answered therefore that [one], "If a sinner he is, not I know; one [thing] I know, that blind being, now I see."

L.25: So that [man] answered, "Whether {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is a sinner, I do not know; one [thing] I know, that being blind, now I see."

R.25: The man answered, "I do not know if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is a sinner. But there is one thing I do know. Before, I could not see. Now I can!"

decisions.choice: whether he is a sinner, I do not know: he will not give the verdict they demand
alternatives: If he is a sinner, I do not know it (a denial that he is one)
decisions.reason: The "if" introduces an indirect question, as often after "know". The man neither agrees nor openly disagrees. He leaves the question of the law to them and holds to what he can say for himself. By 9:31-33 he will draw the conclusion they refuse.

decisions.choice: being blind, now I see: the participle stands for his former state, set against "now"
alternatives: although I am blind, I see
decisions.reason: The present participle describes what he was, a man blind from birth, and "now" marks the change. The sentence sets two plain facts side by side, the whole of his testimony.

decisions.choice: one thing I know: testimony from what he has experienced
decisions.reason: Against their "we know" (9:24) the man sets "I know". John's Gospel is built on testimony from what people have seen and heard (1:34; 3:11; 19:35; 21:24), and this man's testimony is of that kind. He cannot judge theology, but he can say what happened to him.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, whoever is speaking, including the leaders who reject him. This applies throughout the passage. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain.

decisions.choice: I used to be blind, and now I can see (B); Before, I could not see. Now I can! (R)
alternatives: I was blind, but now I see
decisions.reason: The familiar form of these words, made well known by older translations and the hymn "Amazing Grace", adds a "but" and a past tense. Balanced and Readable give the sense of the participle in plain words: what he was before, and what he is now.

records.source: εἶπον οὖν αὐτῷ· Τί ἐποίησέν σοι;
records.gloss: They said therefore to him, "What did he to you?

L.26: So they said to him, "What did {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} do to you?

R.26: Then they asked him, "What did {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} do to you?

decisions.choice: they question him again on the details of the healing
decisions.reason: He has already told them (9:15). The text does not give their reason for asking again. The setting suggests they are looking for a slip or for some detail they can use against Jesus, such as the making of mud on the Sabbath (9:6, 14); the man takes it so (9:27).

decisions.choice: asked
decisions.reason: The words that follow are a question, so Balanced and Readable say "asked".

records.source: πῶς ἤνοιξέν σου τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς;
records.gloss: How opened he of you the eyes?"

R.26: How did {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} make you able to see?"

decisions.choice: open the eyes: give sight
decisions.reason: To open a blind person's eyes is to make them see. The phrase runs through the chapter (9:10, 14, 17, 21, 26, 30, 32) and recalls what God promises to do in Isaiah (35:5; 42:7).

decisions.choice: how: the same question asked again
decisions.reason: The neighbors asked how (9:10), the Pharisees asked how (9:15), the parents were asked how (9:19-21). The repeated question shows that the fact of the healing is no longer in doubt; only its explanation is.

decisions.choice: make you able to see
decisions.reason: "Open your eyes" can sound like lifting the eyelids, or like making someone understand. Readable says what the idiom means (meaning decision m1), and does so each time in the passage.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς· Εἶπον ὑμῖν ἤδη καὶ οὐκ ἠκούσατε· τί πάλιν θέλετε ἀκούειν;
records.gloss: He answered them, "I told you already and not you listened; why again do you want to hear?

L.27: He answered them, "I told you already, and you did not listen; why do you want to hear [it] again?

R.27: He answered, "I already told you, but you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it all over again?

decisions.choice: you did not listen: you heard, but did not take it in or accept it
decisions.reason: They plainly heard his account (9:15). To "hear" in John often means to listen and accept (5:24-25; 8:43, 47; 10:3, 27). The man's complaint is that they did not take his words seriously.

decisions.choice: and you did not listen (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: A few witnesses, among them the papyrus P66 and some Old Latin copies, are reported to leave out "not", which gives "I told you already, and you heard; why do you want to hear it again?" The reading with "not" is found in the great majority of manuscripts. The sense of the sentence is much the same either way. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: why do you want to hear it again: a question that turns their questioning back on them
decisions.reason: The man, under examination, begins to question his examiners. His question leads to the bolder one that follows.

decisions.choice: [it] (L); it (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the object of "hear" unstated; it is his account of the healing.

records.source: μὴ καὶ ὑμεῖς θέλετε αὐτοῦ μαθηταὶ γενέσθαι;
records.gloss: Not also you want of him disciples to become?"

L.27: Surely you also do not want to become {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples?"

R.27: Do you want to be {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples too? Surely not!"

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no, asked with irony
decisions.reason: The word that opens the question expects a denial. The man knows they do not want to follow Jesus; the question needles them for their interest in every detail.

decisions.choice: you also: the man counts himself among those who follow Jesus, or is ready to
alternatives: also, in addition to wanting to hear the story
decisions.reason: "Also" stands with "you": you as well as others. The leaders hear it as a confession that he is already a disciple (9:28). Others had begun to believe in Jesus (7:31; 8:30), and the man may mean them too.

decisions.choice: disciples: followers who learn from a teacher
decisions.reason: A disciple attached himself to a teacher to learn his way. The leaders take up the word at once: they are disciples of Moses (9:28).

decisions.choice: Surely ... do not (L); Could it be that (B); ... Surely not! (R)
alternatives: You do not want to become his disciples too, do you?
decisions.reason: Each level marks the question as expecting a denial (meaning decision m1), so that the man's irony shows.

records.source: ἐλοιδόρησαν αὐτὸν καὶ εἶπον· Σὺ μαθητὴς εἶ ἐκείνου, ἡμεῖς δὲ τοῦ Μωϋσέως ἐσμὲν μαθηταί·
records.gloss: They reviled him and said, "You a disciple are of that [one], we but of the Moses are disciples;

L.28: They reviled him and said, "You are a disciple of that [man], but we are disciples of Moses.

R.28: Then they shouted insults at him. They said, "You are that man's disciple! But we are disciples of Moses.

decisions.choice: reviled: abused him with insulting words
decisions.reason: The verb means to speak abusively of or to someone. They answer his question not with an argument but with scorn.

decisions.choice: you ... that one ... we: emphatic pronouns setting two loyalties apart
decisions.reason: Both "you" and "we" are emphatic, drawing a line between the man and themselves. "That one" keeps Jesus at a distance; they do not speak his name.

decisions.choice: disciples of Moses: faithful to the law God gave through Moses
decisions.reason: The Pharisees saw themselves as students and guardians of Moses' law (7:19, 22-23). They set Moses against Jesus, but John has already said that the law came through Moses and grace and truth through Jesus Christ (1:17), and Jesus has said that Moses wrote about him (5:45-46). To be a true disciple of Moses would be to believe in Jesus.

decisions.choice: that [man] (L); that man (B, R)
decisions.reason: The demonstrative keeps the contempt of their words (meaning decision m2); there is no pronoun for Jesus here, so no setting applies.

records.source: ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν ὅτι Μωϋσεῖ λελάληκεν ὁ θεός, τοῦτον δὲ οὐκ οἴδαμεν πόθεν ἐστίν.
records.gloss: We know that to Moses has spoken the God, this [one] but not we know from where he is."

L.29: We know that God has spoken to Moses, but this [man], we do not know where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is from."

R.29: We know that God spoke to Moses. But this man? We do not know where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes from!"

decisions.choice: has spoken: God spoke to Moses, and that word still stands
decisions.reason: The perfect tense points to God's speaking to Moses as a settled fact with lasting force. Scripture says that God spoke with Moses face to face (Exodus 33:11; Numbers 12:6-8), and the law came from that speaking.

decisions.choice: where he is from: his origin, and so who sent him and by what authority
decisions.reason: To know where a man is from is to know whether his authority is real. Earlier, people in Jerusalem said they knew where Jesus was from (7:27), and Jesus told the Pharisees that they did not know where he came from (8:14). Now the leaders admit it, meaning it as a reason to dismiss him. In John's eyes they have said more than they know: he comes from God (7:29).

decisions.choice: Where this man comes from, we do not know
alternatives: but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "this man" up front, as the Greek does, by starting with the question of his origin.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ τὸ θαυμαστόν ἐστιν ὅτι ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἐστίν, καὶ ἤνοιξέν μου τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς.
records.gloss: Answered the man and said to them, "In this for the amazing [thing] is, that you not know from where he is, and he opened my the eyes.

L.30: The man answered and said to them, "Why, in this is the amazing [thing], that you do not know where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is from, and [yet] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} opened my eyes.

R.30: The man answered, "That is amazing! You do not know where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes from. But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made me able to see!

decisions.choice: for: here it introduces an exclamation, not a reason
decisions.reason: In replies the little word often has the force of "why" or "well then", taking up what was just said with surprise. The man is not giving a reason; he is pointing to the absurdity of their position.

decisions.choice: the amazing thing: something to marvel at, said with irony
decisions.reason: The marvel is not the healing itself but their ignorance. Men who claim to know what God approves cannot explain a deed only God could make possible.

decisions.choice: and: with the sense "and yet"
decisions.reason: The two clauses stand in contrast: they do not know where he is from, and yet he did what only one sent by God could do.

decisions.choice: Why ... [yet] (L); Well ... still (B)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced show the exclamation and the contrast (meaning decisions m1 and m3); Literal brackets "yet".

records.source: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὁ θεὸς οὐκ ἀκούει, ἀλλ’ ἐάν τις θεοσεβὴς ᾖ καὶ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ποιῇ τούτου ἀκούει.
records.gloss: We know that sinners the God not hears, but if anyone God-fearing is and the will of him does, this [one] he hears.

L.31: We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is God-fearing and does {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} will, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} listens to {{gender:them|him}}.

R.31: We know that God does not listen to sinners. But God does listen to people who respect {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wants.

decisions.choice: we know: the man speaks of what everyone, the leaders included, believes
alternatives: we, meaning the man and those who follow Jesus
decisions.reason: He takes up the leaders' own words (9:24, 29) and appeals to a belief they share. From it he will argue to the conclusion they will not accept (9:33).

decisions.choice: God does not listen to sinners: the teaching of the Scriptures
decisions.reason: The Scriptures say that God does not hear those who hold on to sin (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; Isaiah 1:15) and that he hears the prayer of the righteous (Psalm 34:16; Proverbs 15:29). "Sinners" here means people who go on in sin and do not turn from it. The man's point is that God has answered Jesus, so Jesus cannot be a sinner of that kind (compare 11:41-42).

decisions.choice: God-fearing: devout, reverent toward God
decisions.reason: The word describes a person who honors God in worship and in life. It comes only here in the New Testament. Doing God's will is joined to it, as in 7:17.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" includes men and women, so the pronoun that refers back to it takes the gender setting. Readable says "people" and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: reveres God (B); respect him (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the adjective into a verb (meaning decision m3). "Respect" in Readable is meant in the sense of honoring God.

records.source: ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἠκούσθη ὅτι ἠνέῳξέν τις ὀφθαλμοὺς τυφλοῦ γεγεννημένου·
records.gloss: Out of the age not it was heard that opened anyone eyes of [one] blind having been born;

L.32: From of old it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of [someone] born blind.

R.32: From the beginning of time until now, no one has ever heard of anyone making someone who was born blind able to see.

decisions.choice: from the age: never in all of history
decisions.reason: The phrase means from the earliest times. With "not" it says that such a thing has never been heard of. The Scriptures tell of no one who gave sight to a person born blind.

decisions.choice: opening the eyes of the blind: a work the prophets give to God and to his chosen servant
alternatives: no echo of the prophets intended
decisions.reason: Isaiah speaks of a day when the eyes of the blind will be opened (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5), and of God's servant who will open blind eyes (Isaiah 42:7). The man does not quote these, and his point is that the deed is unheard of; but John's readers may hear in it a sign that the promised age has come.

decisions.choice: born blind: blind from birth
decisions.reason: The perfect participle describes a person who was born that way and remained so, as in 9:1. Healing such blindness is what makes the deed unheard of.

decisions.choice: In all the ages (B); From the beginning of time until now (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idiom (meaning decision m1) into plain words.

records.source: εἰ μὴ ἦν οὗτος παρὰ θεοῦ, οὐκ ἠδύνατο ποιεῖν οὐδέν.
records.gloss: If not were this [one] from God, not he could do nothing."

L.33: If this [man] were not from God, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could not do anything."

R.33: If this man had not come from God, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could not do anything like this."

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: he is from God
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence assumes the opposite of the if-clause. The man draws the conclusion of his argument: God does not hear sinners (9:31), this deed is unheard of (9:32), so the one who did it must be from God.

decisions.choice: from God: sent by God, as a prophet is
alternatives: coming from God's own presence (the sense Jesus gives it of himself)
decisions.reason: Some of the Pharisees had said Jesus was "not from God" (9:16), and Nicodemus said he was a teacher come from God (3:2). The man means one sent by God, as he has called Jesus a prophet (9:17). John's readers know that Jesus is from God in a deeper sense still (6:46; 7:29).

decisions.choice: could not do anything: a double negative for emphasis
decisions.reason: "Not" and "nothing" together make the denial strong. In the setting the man means that he could have done nothing like this.

decisions.choice: anything like this
decisions.reason: Readable says what "nothing" refers to in the setting (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθησαν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Ἐν ἁμαρτίαις σὺ ἐγεννήθης ὅλος, καὶ σὺ διδάσκεις ἡμᾶς;
records.gloss: They answered and said to him, "In sins you were born wholly, and you teach us?"

L.34: They answered and said to him, "You were born entirely in sins, and you are teaching us?"

R.34: They answered, "You were born completely in sin! And you are trying to teach us?"

decisions.choice: born in sins: they take his blindness from birth as proof that he was born under sin
decisions.reason: They assume what the disciples assumed (9:2), that a man born blind bears the mark of sin, and what Jesus denied (9:3). Without meaning to, they also admit that he was born blind, which they had doubted (9:18).

decisions.choice: entirely: the whole of him, every part
decisions.reason: The word stands with "you": not merely touched by sin, but wholly sinful from birth.

decisions.choice: and you teach us?: a scornful question, with "you" emphatic
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out twice. The question means: someone like you has no right to teach men like us. The present tense describes what he is doing, or attempting.

decisions.choice: in sin through and through (B); completely in sin (R)
decisions.reason: "Sin" in the singular is the natural way to speak of a sinful state; Literal keeps the plural.

decisions.choice: trying to
decisions.reason: Readable shows the scorn of the question (meaning decision m3): he is attempting something they think he has no standing to do.

records.source: καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω.
records.gloss: And they threw him outside.

decisions.choice: threw him out: drove him from their presence, and probably from the synagogue community as well
alternatives: only out of the room or court where they questioned him
a formal sentence of expulsion from the synagogue
decisions.reason: The words say that they forced him out. His parents had feared the decision that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue (9:22; compare 12:42; 16:2), and the man has just defended Jesus as one from God. The text does not say whether a formal sentence was passed, but the result was that he was cut off from them. A footnote gives the narrower reading.

decisions.choice: thrown out by the leaders, then found by Jesus
decisions.reason: The same words are used in 6:37, where Jesus says that whoever comes to him he will never throw out. Those who reject the man cast him out; in the next verse Jesus goes looking for him (9:35), as the good shepherd seeks his sheep (10:3-4).

decisions.choice: threw him out
decisions.reason: "Threw him out" keeps both senses open, out of the room and out of the community (meaning decision m1), as the Greek does.

records.source: Ἤκουσεν Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω, καὶ εὑρὼν αὐτὸν εἶπεν· Σὺ πιστεύεις εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου;
records.gloss: Heard Jesus that they had thrown him out, and having found him he said, "You, do you believe in the Son of the man?"

L.35: Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and having found him, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"

R.35: Jesus heard that the leaders had thrown the man out. So Jesus went and found him and asked, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"

decisions.choice: the Son of Man (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the Son of God (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "the Son of God". The oldest witnesses, among them two early papyri, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read "the Son of Man", the title Jesus uses of himself throughout John. A change from the unusual question about the Son of Man to the more familiar confession of the Son of God is easier to explain than the reverse. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they threw him out: the leaders drove him from their presence, and with it, in the light of 9:22, from the synagogue community
alternatives: they only sent him out of the room
a formal sentence of expulsion pronounced on the spot
decisions.reason: The words repeat the end of verse 34. They at least mean that the Pharisees put him out of their presence in contempt. John has already said that the authorities had agreed to put out of the synagogue anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ (9:22), so the reader is meant to see the man suffering what his parents feared. John does not describe any formal procedure.

decisions.choice: Jesus seeks the man out
decisions.reason: As with the man healed at the pool (5:14), it is Jesus who finds the man after the healing. The one the authorities have thrown out is sought and received by Jesus (compare 6:37; 10:3-4).

decisions.choice: you, do you believe: the pronoun is emphatic
alternatives: a plain question with no stress on the person
decisions.reason: The Greek states "you" where the verb alone would do. It sets the man over against the Pharisees who have refused to believe: whatever they think, does he believe?

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus's title for himself
alternatives: a general expression for a human being
decisions.reason: In John the Son of Man is the one who comes down from heaven and is lifted up (1:51; 3:13-14; 8:28), and the one to whom the Father has given authority to judge (5:27). That last point prepares for verse 39. The title draws on Daniel 7:13-14. The man does not yet know that Jesus is speaking of himself (verse 36).
