decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including the pronouns for the Son of Man in verse 36, since the one asked about is Jesus (as with the coming Messiah at 4:25 and 7:27), and "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: the leaders; So Jesus went and found him
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" were, the leaders who questioned the man in verses 13-34, and makes plain that Jesus went looking for him (meaning decision m3).

records.heading: Those who see and those who are blind

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη ἐκεῖνος καὶ εἶπεν· Καὶ τίς ἐστιν, κύριε, ἵνα πιστεύσω εἰς αὐτόν;
records.gloss: Answered that [one] and said, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?"

L.36: That [man] answered and said, "And who is {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, Sir, so that I may believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"

R.36: The man answered, "Sir, who is {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}? I want to believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: Sir: a respectful address
alternatives: Lord, a confession of who Jesus is
decisions.reason: The word is the polite form used to anyone of standing, as the Samaritan woman uses it (4:11, 15, 19). The man already holds Jesus to be a prophet (9:17) and sent from God (9:33), but he does not yet know who the Son of Man is, or that he is speaking to him. In verse 38, once he believes, the same word carries the full sense of "Lord". A footnote gives "Lord".

decisions.choice: and who is he, so that I may believe: an eager question; he is ready to believe once he knows
decisions.reason: The opening "and" gives the question urgency, and the clause of purpose shows why he asks: he wants to know whom to believe in. He does not refuse the question; he asks to be shown.

decisions.choice: he and him: the Son of Man, who is Jesus himself
decisions.reason: The man asks about a third person, but the reader knows the answer, and verse 37 gives it: the one he is speaking to.

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: Shows the polite address (meaning decision m1), so that the change to "Lord" in verse 38 can be seen.

decisions.choice: Tell me, so that
decisions.reason: Balanced breaks the question in two and supplies "Tell me", which the clause of purpose implies (meaning decision m2).

records.source: εἶπεν αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Καὶ ἑώρακας αὐτὸν καὶ ὁ λαλῶν μετὰ σοῦ ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Said to him the Jesus, "Both you have seen him, and the [one] speaking with you, that [one] is."

L.37: Jesus said to him, "You have both seen {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and the one speaking with you is that [one]."

R.37: Jesus said to him, "You have seen {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} with your own eyes. He is the one talking with you right now."

decisions.choice: you have seen him: the man who was blind has now seen the Son of Man
alternatives: only a figure of speech for knowing him
decisions.reason: The man was sent away to wash before he could see (9:7), so this is the first time he has seen Jesus. The perfect tense stresses that the seeing has happened and stands. The words also prepare for verse 39: his eyes see, and now he is coming to see who Jesus is.

decisions.choice: the one speaking with you is he: Jesus reveals himself as he did to the Samaritan woman
decisions.reason: The words echo 4:26, where Jesus tells the woman that the Messiah she expects is the one speaking with her. In both places Jesus makes himself known to someone who has asked.

decisions.choice: both ... and: two ways of meeting him, seeing and hearing
alternatives: the first "and" as a mere connective
decisions.reason: The paired "and ... and" joins the two clauses: he has seen him, and he is hearing him now. The emphatic "that one" points from the Son of Man asked about to the speaker.

decisions.choice: is that [one]
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek pointing word "that one" at the end; Balanced turns it round to the natural order.

decisions.choice: with your own eyes; right now
decisions.reason: Readable brings out that the man is now seeing with eyes that were blind (meaning decision m1), and that the speaker is present before him.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἔφη· Πιστεύω, κύριε· καὶ προσεκύνησεν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: He then said, "I believe, lord"; and he worshiped him.

L.38: And he said, "I believe, Lord." And he worshiped {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.38: The man said, "I believe, Lord!" And he bowed down and worshiped {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the words are part of the text (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the words "He said, 'I believe, Lord,' and he worshiped him. And Jesus said" (verses 38 and the start of 39) are missing
decisions.reason: A few early witnesses, among them an early papyrus (P75), the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex W, lack this verse and the opening words of verse 39, so that Jesus's words in verse 39 follow straight on from verse 37. Almost all other manuscripts have them, and the SBLGNT prints them. A footnote notes the omission. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Lord: now an address of faith
alternatives: Sir, a polite address as in verse 36
decisions.reason: It is the same word the man used in verse 36, but he now says it as he confesses his faith in the Son of Man. Those who have come to believe call Jesus "Lord" (6:68; 11:27; 20:28). The word is the same; what has changed is the man who says it.

decisions.choice: worshiped: bowed down before him in worship
alternatives: knelt before him in respect, as before an honored human
decisions.reason: The verb means to bow down before someone, and it can be used of homage to a human superior (Matthew 18:26). In John, though, it is used only of worshiping God (4:20-24; 12:20), and here it follows a confession of faith in the Son of Man. A footnote gives "knelt before him".

decisions.choice: I believe: the end of the man's journey from blindness to faith
decisions.reason: Step by step the man has spoken of "the man called Jesus" (9:11), "a prophet" (9:17) and one "from God" (9:33); now he believes and worships. The Pharisees have moved the other way, from questions to rejection, as verses 39-41 bring out.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The address changes from "Sir" (verse 36) to "Lord" because the man now believes (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: bowed down and worshiped
decisions.reason: Readable shows the bodily act the verb describes as well as its sense (meaning decision m3).

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Εἰς κρίμα ἐγὼ εἰς τὸν κόσμον τοῦτον ἦλθον, ἵνα οἱ μὴ βλέποντες βλέπωσιν καὶ οἱ βλέποντες τυφλοὶ γένωνται.
records.gloss: And said the Jesus, "For judgment I into the world this came, that the [ones] not seeing may see and the [ones] seeing blind may become."

L.39: And Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, so that the [ones] not seeing may see, and the [ones] seeing may become blind."

R.39: Jesus said, "I came into this world to bring judgment. I came so that people who are blind can see, and people who think they can see will become blind."

decisions.choice: judgment: a verdict that separates people, brought about by his coming
alternatives: condemnation as the aim of his coming
the act of judging in a court
decisions.reason: The word is the result of judging, a verdict. Here it is the division that Jesus's coming brings about between those who come to see and those who refuse to.

decisions.choice: his coming brings judgment, though he did not come to condemn
decisions.reason: In 3:17 God did not send the Son to judge the world but to save it, and in 12:47 Jesus says the same. Yet the Father has given all judgment to the Son (5:22, 27), and 3:19 explains how both are true: the light has come, and people's response to it is itself the judgment. Here the man who was blind has come to the light, and the Pharisees have turned from it.

decisions.choice: so that: the purpose of his coming, which is also its outcome
decisions.reason: The conjunction normally states a purpose. Jesus came to give sight; that those who claim to see become blind is the other side of the same coming, as light that shows the way also exposes those who turn away from it (3:19-21).

decisions.choice: giving sight to the blind and blinding those who see: echoes of Isaiah
decisions.reason: Isaiah promises that the eyes of the blind will be opened (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7), and speaks of a people who see but do not perceive, whose eyes are shut (Isaiah 6:9-10, quoted in John 12:40; compare 42:18-19).

decisions.choice: seeing and blindness in two senses: the body's eyes and understanding of God
decisions.reason: The whole chapter turns on this. The man born blind receives his sight and comes to see who Jesus is; the Pharisees, who can see and claim to know (9:24, 29), become blind to him. Those who "see" are those who think they see (verse 41).

decisions.choice: to bring judgment
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what "for judgment" means (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: people who think they can see
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit that the seeing is claimed, as Jesus says in verse 41 (meaning decision m5).

records.source: ἤκουσαν ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων ταῦτα οἱ μετ’ αὐτοῦ ὄντες, καὶ εἶπον αὐτῷ· Μὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς τυφλοί ἐσμεν;
records.gloss: Heard [some] of the Pharisees these things, the [ones] with him being, and they said to him, "Not also we blind are?"

L.40: [Some] of the Pharisees who were with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} heard these things, and they said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "We are not blind too, are we?"

R.40: Some of the Pharisees who were there with Jesus heard this. They said to Jesus, "You are not saying that we are blind too, are you?"

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: The question begins with a particle that looks for a denial. The Pharisees do not ask whether they are blind; they object that Jesus cannot be saying so.

decisions.choice: we too: we as well as others he calls blind
decisions.reason: The stress falls on "we": they assume that blindness belongs to people like the man they have just called a sinner (9:34), not to teachers of the Law.

decisions.choice: who were with him: who were present with Jesus at the time
decisions.reason: The phrase means only that they were there. These Pharisees were not his disciples (9:28); they heard what he said to the man.

decisions.choice: You do not mean that ... do you? (B); You are not saying that ... are you? (R)
decisions.reason: The English puts the expected "no" into the question (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: [Some] of
decisions.reason: The Greek says "of the Pharisees", meaning some of them; Literal brackets the supplied word.

records.source: εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Εἰ τυφλοὶ ἦτε, οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν· νῦν δὲ λέγετε ὅτι Βλέπομεν· ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑμῶν μένει.
records.gloss: Said to them the Jesus, "If blind you were, not would you have sin; now but you say that, 'We see'; the sin of you remains."

L.41: Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, 'We see'; your sin remains."

R.41: Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin. But you say, 'We can see.' So your sin remains."

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: they are not blind in the way that would excuse them
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence assumes that the condition is not true. They are not people who cannot see; they claim to see.

decisions.choice: to have sin: to be guilty of sin
decisions.reason: John uses the phrase for guilt that a person must answer for (15:22, 24; 19:11). Those who truly could not see would not be held guilty for failing to see.

decisions.choice: their sin is claiming sight while refusing it
alternatives: they are guilty because of what they know
decisions.reason: The Pharisees claim to know (9:24, 29) and yet refuse the light that has come (3:19-20). Their claim to see leaves them no excuse; in the same way Jesus says that those who do not believe will die in their sins (8:24).

decisions.choice: remains: stays on them and is not taken away
decisions.reason: The verb is the one John uses for what lasts. As God's wrath remains on whoever refuses to obey the Son (3:36), so their sin remains, because they turn from the one who takes away the sin of the world (1:29).

decisions.choice: would have no sin (B); would not be guilty of sin (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what having sin means here (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: so
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "so" to show that their sin remains because of their claim, which the Greek implies by setting the two clauses side by side.
